claim: Cell division is fundamental to all healthy tissue growth.
source: Cell division is fundamental to all healthy tissue growth, as well as being rate-limiting in the tissue repair response to wounding and during cancer progression.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cell division is rate-limiting in the tissue repair response to wounding.
source: Cell division is fundamental to all healthy tissue growth, as well as being rate-limiting in the tissue repair response to wounding and during cancer progression.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cell division is rate-limiting during cancer progression.
source: Cell division is fundamental to all healthy tissue growth, as well as being rate-limiting in the tissue repair response to wounding and during cancer progression.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The role that cell divisions play in tissue growth is a collective one, requiring the integration of many individual cell division events.
source: However, the role that cell divisions play in tissue growth is a collective one, requiring the integration of many individual cell division events.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract.

claim: It is particularly difficult to accurately detect and quantify multiple features of large numbers of cell divisions over extended periods of time.
source: It is particularly difficult to accurately detect and quantify multiple features of large numbers of cell divisions (including their spatio-temporal synchronicity and orientation) over extended periods of time.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field in the abstract.

claim: The authors developed a pipeline of deep learning models that accurately identify dividing cells in time-lapse movies of epithelial tissues in vivo.
source: Hence, we develop a pipeline of deep learning models that accurately identify dividing cells in time-lapse movies of epithelial tissues in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with model performance metrics.

claim: The deep learning pipeline determines the axis of division orientation.
source: Our pipeline also determines their axis of division orientation, as well as their shape changes before and after division.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the manuscript with the U-NetOrientation model.

claim: The deep learning pipeline determines shape changes of cells before and after division.
source: Our pipeline also determines their axis of division orientation, as well as their shape changes before and after division.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with the U-NetBoundary model in the manuscript.

claim: The division axis is biased according to lines of tissue tension in the Drosophila pupal wing epithelium.
source: We show that the division axis is biased according to lines of tissue tension and that wounding triggers a synchronised (but not oriented) burst of cell divisions back from the leading edge.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Wounding triggers a synchronised burst of cell divisions back from the leading edge.
source: We show that the division axis is biased according to lines of tissue tension and that wounding triggers a synchronised (but not oriented) burst of cell divisions back from the leading edge.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The wound-induced burst of cell divisions is not oriented.
source: We show that the division axis is biased according to lines of tissue tension and that wounding triggers a synchronised (but not oriented) burst of cell divisions back from the leading edge.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Significant advancements in confocal microscopy make it possible to collect vast quantities of time-lapse imaging data from living tissues as they develop in vivo.
source: Significant advancements in confocal microscopy mean it is now possible to collect vast quantities of time-lapse imaging data from living tissues as they develop in vivo and respond to genetic or environmental perturbations (such as wounding).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: New methodologies are required to efficiently analyse time-lapse movies and extract detailed information about cell behaviours.
source: In parallel with the development of these imaging technologies, new methodologies are required to efficiently analyse these movies and extract detailed information about how the various cell behaviours (e.g., cell movements, divisions, etc.) contribute to tissue development and expansion, and how they enable repair responses following tissue damage (Etournay et al., 2015; Nestor-Bergmann et al., 2019; Olenik et al., 2023; Park et al., 2017; Scarpa et al., 2018; Tetley et al., 2019; Turley et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a need in the field and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Computer vision has progressed extensively in recent years, particularly with the development of deep learning models.
source: Computer vision (a form of artificial intelligence, AI) has progressed extensively in recent years, particularly with the development of deep learning models (Guo et al., 2016; Voulodimos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Deep learning models can be trained to identify and classify objects in images.
source: Such models can be trained to identify and classify objects in images, for example, enabling automated identification of tumours in MRI (Magnetic resonance imaging) scans or segmentation of cells according to their type (Işın et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Deep learning algorithms are particularly useful when analysing medical and biological data because these data are often inherently 'noisy'.
source: These algorithms are particularly useful when analysing medical and biological data (Jones et al., 2017), because these data are often inherently 'noisy', as objects within a class can exhibit significant variation.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale and supported by a citation.

claim: Deep learning algorithms excel at finding patterns in complex data.
source: Deep learning algorithms excel at finding patterns in complex data (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Abstract patterns learned by deep learning algorithms are often so complicated that they are difficult for the human eye to discern.
source: These abstract patterns are often so complicated that they are difficult for the human eye to discern (Bhatt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of deep learning and supported by a citation.

claim: Deep learning algorithms must 'learn' from 'labelled data' in order to operate.
source: In order to operate, deep learning algorithms must 'learn' from 'labelled data', that is, data in which an expert has already performed the task that we require the model to automate (e.g., segmentation, classification, etc.).
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental principle of deep learning.

claim: Deep learning algorithms can be highly accurate at performing relatively simple vision tasks and are often much quicker than when the equivalent task is performed manually.
source: The resulting algorithms can be highly accurate at performing relatively simple vision tasks and are often much quicker than when the equivalent task is performed manually (Jones et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of deep learning and supported by a citation.

claim: The high consistency of deep learning models reduces operator bias and can guarantee the same level of accuracy across all experiments and studies.
source: Furthermore, the high consistency of the resulting models reduces operator bias (or error) and can guarantee the same level of accuracy across all experiments and studies.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of deep learning.

claim: In microscopy, deep learning has largely been applied to static images.
source: In microscopy, deep learning has, so far, largely been applied to static images and has enabled relatively simple analyses, such as cell counting and quantification of object area (or volume), as well as more sophisticated tasks, such as the capacity to distinguish different cell types (Jones et al., 2017), and for detection of mitotic indexes in biopsy tissue sections which have notoriously poor manual reproducibility (Aubreville et al., 2020; Piansaddhayanaon et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated as the current state of the field and supported by citations.

claim: AI approaches are increasingly employed in and beginning to revolutionise digital pathology.
source: AI approaches are increasingly employed in (and beginning to revolutionise) digital pathology (Burlutskiy et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022), and whilst most current applications are to two-dimensional (2D) static images, there are opportunities for deep learning models to be applied to dynamic time-lapse videos.
evidence: This is stated as a trend in the field and supported by citations.

claim: The Drosophila pupal epithelium is densely packed with nuclei.
source: The biological tissue we investigate – the Drosophila pupal epithelium – is densely packed with nuclei, and the developmental cell divisions are dispersed and rapid, each occurring over a period of only several minutes.
evidence: This is a description of the biological system used in the study.

claim: Developmental cell divisions in the Drosophila pupal epithelium are dispersed and rapid, each occurring over a period of only several minutes.
source: The biological tissue we investigate – the Drosophila pupal epithelium – is densely packed with nuclei, and the developmental cell divisions are dispersed and rapid, each occurring over a period of only several minutes.
evidence: This is a description of the biological system used in the study.

claim: The pupal epithelium is somewhat prone to photo-bleaching, limiting the frequency at which sequential images can be collected whilst maintaining tissue health.
source: Moreover, as with most fluorescently labelled live tissue, the pupal epithelium is somewhat prone to photo-bleaching, thus limiting the frequency at which sequential images can be collected whilst maintaining tissue health.
evidence: This is stated as a constraint of the imaging system.

claim: Standard methods for tracking nuclei (such as TrackMate) failed to cope with the constraints of the in vivo imaging data.
source: We found that standard methods for tracking nuclei (such as TrackMate; Tinevez et al., 2017) failed to cope with the constraints of our in vivo imaging data and routinely confused epithelial cell divisions with migrating immune cells (that often contain nuclear material from engulfed apoptotic corpses), whilst also missing many mitotic events that are clear to the eye.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods and supported by a citation.

claim: Cell divisions in time-lapse movie data produce unique and reproducible patterns of motion.
source: However, whilst cell divisions in time-lapse movie data are often too dynamic for current methods for cell tracking, they do produce unique and reproducible patterns of motion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivates the use of deep learning.

claim: Previous work on automated methods for detecting cell divisions has largely been performed on lower-density tissues with cells spread relatively far apart and mostly in vitro.
source: Previous work on automated methods for detecting cell divisions has largely been performed on lower-density tissues with cells spread relatively far apart and mostly in vitro (Gilad et al., 2019; Kitrungrotsakul et al., 2021; Nie et al., 2016; Phan et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work and supported by citations.

claim: Many existing models for detecting cell divisions are not accurate enough for biologists to analyse more complex in vivo data.
source: Whilst considerable progress has been made over the years, many of these models are not accurate enough for biologists to analyse more complex in vivo data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Unsupervised methods for detecting cell divisions have the major advantage of not needing time-consuming hand labelling of data.
source: Some existing approaches use unsupervised methods, which have the major advantage of not needing time-consuming hand labelling of data; however, these methods may struggle to cope with highly dense tissues and currently perform worse (i.e., exhibit a lower accuracy of detection) than supervised models (Gilad et al., 2019; Phan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of unsupervised methods and supported by citations.

claim: Unsupervised methods for detecting cell divisions currently perform worse than supervised models.
source: Some existing approaches use unsupervised methods, which have the major advantage of not needing time-consuming hand labelling of data; however, these methods may struggle to cope with highly dense tissues and currently perform worse (i.e., exhibit a lower accuracy of detection) than supervised models (Gilad et al., 2019; Phan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison of methods and supported by citations.

claim: The authors propose a simpler, direct single deep learning model that can detect cell divisions with high accuracy even with challenging conditions.
source: Here, we propose a simpler, direct single deep learning model that can detect cell divisions with high accuracy even with challenging conditions that require it to cope with very dense and dynamic (developing) tissues as well as with wound-induced debris.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the model developed in the study, supported by performance metrics in Table 1.

claim: The model achieves high accuracy by using much deeper networks based on highly effective and widely used image classifying models.
source: This is achieved by using much deeper networks, based on highly effective and widely used image classifying models, and by increasing input information (e.g. using two independent fluorescent channels), which we show increases model accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach and supported by the model architecture description and performance data.

claim: Using two independent fluorescent channels increases model accuracy.
source: This is achieved by using much deeper networks, based on highly effective and widely used image classifying models, and by increasing input information (e.g. using two independent fluorescent channels), which we show increases model accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by comparison of model performance in Table 1.

claim: In the unwounded developing pupal epithelium, cell division density decreases linearly with time.
source: As expected, in the unwounded developing pupal epithelium, we observe that cell division density decreases linearly with time (Etournay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous work and supported by data in Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: Wounding triggers a synchronous burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding.
source: However, wounding triggers a synchronous burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding, in a ring of epithelial tissue beginning several cell diameters back from the wound edge; this ring of proliferation becomes broader with increased wound size.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: The wound-induced burst of cell divisions occurs in a ring of epithelial tissue beginning several cell diameters back from the wound edge.
source: However, wounding triggers a synchronous burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding, in a ring of epithelial tissue beginning several cell diameters back from the wound edge; this ring of proliferation becomes broader with increased wound size.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The ring of proliferation following wounding becomes broader with increased wound size.
source: However, wounding triggers a synchronous burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding, in a ring of epithelial tissue beginning several cell diameters back from the wound edge; this ring of proliferation becomes broader with increased wound size.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data comparing small and large wounds in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The authors chose to develop and test their model using the epithelium of the Drosophila pupal wing because of the optical translucency and genetic tractability of Drosophila.
source: We chose to develop, and test the capability of, our model using the epithelium of the Drosophila pupal wing because of the optical translucency and genetic tractability of Drosophila, which makes it easy to generate tissues with fluorescently labelled nuclei and cell boundaries (Etournay et al., 2015; George and Martin, 2022; Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the choice of model system and supported by citations.

claim: The Drosophila pupal wing epithelium undergoes extensive growth through rapid cell divisions early in pupal life.
source: The Drosophila pupal wing epithelium undergoes extensive growth through rapid cell divisions early in pupal life (Athilingam et al., 2021; Paci and Mao, 2021), and can be imaged with high spatio-temporal resolution using live confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the model system and supported by citations.

claim: The Drosophila pupal wing epithelium can be imaged with high spatio-temporal resolution using live confocal microscopy.
source: The Drosophila pupal wing epithelium undergoes extensive growth through rapid cell divisions early in pupal life (Athilingam et al., 2021; Paci and Mao, 2021), and can be imaged with high spatio-temporal resolution using live confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the model system.

claim: The wing epithelium is a relatively flat 2D cell sheet, composed of two opposing cell layers, each one-cell thick.
source: The wing epithelium is a relatively flat 2D cell sheet, composed of two opposing cell layers, each one-cell thick.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the tissue structure.

claim: An ablation laser is used to generate sterile and reproducible wounds which heal rapidly within a few hours.
source: To analyse the cell behaviours involved in tissue repair, we use an ablation laser to generate sterile and reproducible wounds which heal rapidly within a few hours (Weavers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a method and supported by a citation.

claim: The authors performed time-lapse imaging of unwounded and wounded pupal wings, with each movie lasting 3 hr.
source: To gather training data to build an algorithm that can reliably detect cell divisions, we performed time-lapse imaging of unwounded and wounded pupal wings, with each movie lasting 3 hr (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated as a method.

claim: The wounds generated possessed a mean radius of 20 μm (ranging from 9 to 30 μm).
source: For the wounded imaging data, the wounds generated possessed a mean radius of 20 μm (ranging from 9 to 30 μm), with the smallest wounds closing 20 min after wounding and the largest wounds taking up to 90 min to fully close.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental data.

claim: The smallest wounds close 20 min after wounding.
source: For the wounded imaging data, the wounds generated possessed a mean radius of 20 μm (ranging from 9 to 30 μm), with the smallest wounds closing 20 min after wounding and the largest wounds taking up to 90 min to fully close.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental data.

claim: The largest wounds take up to 90 min to fully close.
source: For the wounded imaging data, the wounds generated possessed a mean radius of 20 μm (ranging from 9 to 30 μm), with the smallest wounds closing 20 min after wounding and the largest wounds taking up to 90 min to fully close.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental data.

claim: Wounding led to the epithelium around the wound edge moving out of the original focal plane which reduced the image quality at the immediate wound edge.
source: Firstly, wounding led to the epithelium around the wound edge moving out of the original focal plane which reduced the image quality at the immediate wound edge.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the imaging data.

claim: There is a wound-associated reduction in the levels of the Ecadherin-GFP junctional reporter.
source: This loss of image quality was further exacerbated by a wound-associated reduction in the levels of the Ecadherin-GFP junctional reporter (Figure 1E, F), which might be a consequence of the previously reported loosening of junctions in the migratory wound epithelium (Martin and Nunan, 2015; Razzell et al., 2014; Tetley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: The wound-associated reduction in Ecadherin-GFP might be a consequence of the previously reported loosening of junctions in the migratory wound epithelium.
source: This loss of image quality was further exacerbated by a wound-associated reduction in the levels of the Ecadherin-GFP junctional reporter (Figure 1E, F), which might be a consequence of the previously reported loosening of junctions in the migratory wound epithelium (Martin and Nunan, 2015; Razzell et al., 2014; Tetley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation supported by citations.

claim: Wounding leads to the accumulation of local tissue debris, including bright nuclear material.
source: Secondly, wounding, by definition, leads to the accumulation of local tissue debris, including bright nuclear material.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Motile immune cells and fat body cells with Histone2Av-mRFP-positive nuclei are recruited to the wound.
source: Motile immune cells and fat body cells, also with Histone2Av-mRFP-positive nuclei, are recruited to the wound and both of these cell lineages engulf tissue debris (Franz et al., 2018; Razzell et al., 2011); these motile and phagocytic (non-epithelial) cell types can be mistaken for dividing epithelial cells providing many opportunities for 'false positives'.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and supported by citations.

claim: Immune cells and fat body cells engulf tissue debris at the wound.
source: Motile immune cells and fat body cells, also with Histone2Av-mRFP-positive nuclei, are recruited to the wound and both of these cell lineages engulf tissue debris (Franz et al., 2018; Razzell et al., 2011); these motile and phagocytic (non-epithelial) cell types can be mistaken for dividing epithelial cells providing many opportunities for 'false positives'.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and supported by citations.

claim: The authors chose to capture images every 2 min to limit photo-bleaching of biological samples.
source: To limit photo-bleaching of our biological samples, we chose to capture images every 2 min (Figure 1E, F), which affords the sample over 1 min of photo-recovery in between scans.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice.

claim: The chromosomal separation phase of cell division (anaphase) takes approximately 6 min in the pupal wing epithelium.
source: Since the chromosomal separation phase of cell division (termed anaphase) takes approximately 6 min in this specific tissue, the chosen imaging frequency captures some details of each division, but is insufficient for the application of a standard (non-deep learning) algorithm.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the biological system.

claim: Particle tracking algorithms are inappropriate for tracking cell divisions in the pupal epithelium because dividing daughter nuclei would frequently be mistakenly linked to a neighbouring nucleus.
source: Particle tracking algorithms, which link nuclei together by the distance travelled, are also inappropriate here, since the pupal epithelial cells (and thus nuclei) are packed close together and dividing daughter nuclei would frequently (and mistakenly) be linked to a neighbouring nucleus rather than being associated with the parental cell.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: The authors use a ResNet34 model modified into a U-Net structure.
source: We use a ResNet34 model modified into a U-Net structure (He et al., 2016; Ronneberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach and supported by citations.

claim: ResNet is a widely used architecture for RGB image classification.
source: ResNet is a widely used architecture for red, green and blue (RGB) image classification.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: ResNet models are constructed of 'residual' layers.
source: These deep learning models, with a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, are constructed of 'residual' layers (hence the name ResNet).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model architecture.

claim: Residual layers are specifically used to overcome the problem of degradation in which adding more layers makes optimising a model more difficult.
source: Residual layers are specifically used to overcome the problem of degradation in which adding more layers makes optimising a model more difficult.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of residual layers.

claim: Residual layers make it possible to construct networks with hundreds of convolutional layers.
source: These layers make it possible to construct networks with hundreds of convolutional layers, which allows deeper networks to be trained and thereby increases the networks' ability to accurately classify images (He et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of residual layers and supported by a citation.

claim: U-Nets were developed to segment images by classifying regions into categories.
source: We defined the time of division as the moment that anaphase starts. We use only 89 (and not all 93) time slices because we have incomplete information about division at the beginning and end of the video.
evidence: This is stated as a description of U-Net architecture.

claim: U-Nets have a U-shaped structure, with an encoder side that applies CNNs and other types of layers which decrease the spatial resolution whilst increasing features.
source: These neural networks have a U-shaped structure, with an encoder side that applies CNNs and other types of layers which decrease the spatial resolution whilst increasing features.
evidence: This is stated as a description of U-Net architecture.

claim: The authors used the fast.ai libraries Dynamic U-Net class which can create a U-Net structure from an image classifier.
source: To boost the model's capacity to segment time-lapse videos, we used the fast.ai libraries Dynamic U-Net class which can create a U-Net structure from an image classifier (see Materials and methods for further details of the model architecture).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach.

claim: A key benefit of the Dynamic U-Net method is that deeper/newer image classifier models can be swapped for more difficult tasks or to increase performance.
source: A key benefit of this method is that deeper/newer image classifier models can be swapped for more difficult tasks or to increase performance.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: The clearest features of a dividing cell occur as the duplicated chromosomes separate and move in opposite directions (observed in the Histone2Av-mRFP channel).
source: The clearest features of a dividing cell occur as the duplicated chromosomes separate and move in opposite directions (observed in the Histone2Av-mRFP channel, arrows, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The authors manually identified dividing cells in 20 independent time-lapse videos of unwounded and wounded tissue to train the model.
source: To train the model, we first manually identified dividing cells in 20 independent time-lapse videos of unwounded and wounded tissue (this generates 'labelled' training data); each training video consisted of 93 time frames (reflecting 186 min of footage).
evidence: This is stated as a method.

claim: The training data contained 4206 divisions in total across all movies.
source: In this training data, we detected 4206 divisions in total across all movies.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the training data.

claim: U-NetCellDivision3 detects only 78.7% of all cell divisions.
source: Dice scores for our algorithm 'U-NetCellDivision3' indicate that this model detects only 78.7% of all cell divisions, and it led to many false positives (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: U-NetCellDivision10 has a dice score above 0.95.
source: As shown in Table 1, there is now a significant (over 80%) reduction in both false positive and false negatives using the 10-frame model. Most of the errors described previously have largely been resolved; a dice score above 0.95 means we can be far more confident in the results produced by U-NetCellDivision10.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: There is a significant (over 80%) reduction in both false positive and false negatives using the 10-frame model compared to the 3-frame model.
source: As shown in Table 1, there is now a significant (over 80%) reduction in both false positive and false negatives using the 10-frame model.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Cells are more likely to divide close to and soon after previous divisions in the unwounded pupal epithelium.
source: Interestingly, in the unwounded pupal epithelium, we observed that cells are more likely to divide close to and soon after previous divisions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a high correlation of cell divisions within a 30-μm radius and temporally, within 40 min in unwounded tissue.
source: There is a high correlation close to the origin (within a 30-μm radius and temporally, within 40 min), which implies that cells are more likely to divide close to others in both space and time; this effect reduces with both increasing distance and time between cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: For larger wounds (15–20 μm radius), there are initially significantly fewer cell divisions in the wounded epithelium compared to unwounded tissues.
source: For larger wounds (15–20 μm radius), there are initially significantly fewer cell divisions (i.e., a lower division density) in the wounded epithelium compared to unwounded tissues (Figure 3C); this wound-associated inhibition of cell division reaches its low point at 60–70 min post-wounding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: The wound-associated inhibition of cell division reaches its low point at 60–70 min post-wounding for large wounds.
source: For larger wounds (15–20 μm radius), there are initially significantly fewer cell divisions (i.e., a lower division density) in the wounded epithelium compared to unwounded tissues (Figure 3C); this wound-associated inhibition of cell division reaches its low point at 60–70 min post-wounding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Smaller wounds (8–12 μm radius) do not exhibit a similar reduction in cell divisions immediately following wounding.
source: In contrast, smaller wounds (8–12 μm radius) do not exhibit a similar reduction in cell divisions immediately following wounding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Both small and large wounds exhibit a dramatic synchronised burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding, double that of unwounded tissue at the peak of this proliferative surge.
source: However, both small and large wounds exhibit a subsequent and dramatic synchronised burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding, double that of unwounded tissue at the peak of this proliferative surge (Figure 3C); after 3 hr post-wounding, the division density of wounded tissue returns to unwounded levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: After 3 hr post-wounding, the division density of wounded tissue returns to unwounded levels.
source: However, both small and large wounds exhibit a subsequent and dramatic synchronised burst of cell divisions at 100 min post-wounding, double that of unwounded tissue at the peak of this proliferative surge (Figure 3C); after 3 hr post-wounding, the division density of wounded tissue returns to unwounded levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: For small wounds, there is a clear decrease in divisions extending up to 20 μm (approximately 5-cell diameters) back from the wound edge until 70 min post-wounding.
source: For small wounds, there is a clear decrease in divisions extending up to 20 μm (approximately 5-cell diameters) back from the wound edge until 70 min post-wounding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: In large wounds, the reduction in division density extends much further back from the wound edge, beyond even the field of view (i.e., greater than 100 μm, approximately 25-cell diameters).
source: In large wounds, this reduction in division density extends much further back from the wound edge, beyond even the field of view (i.e., greater than 100 μm, approximately 25-cell diameters).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: The synchronised burst of divisions occurs between 20 and 70 μm back from the edge of small wounds.
source: The subsequent synchronised burst of divisions occurs between 20 and 70 μm back from the edge of small wounds and extends beyond 100 μm across the whole field of view for large wounds (Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3E and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: The synchronised burst of divisions extends beyond 100 μm across the whole field of view for large wounds.
source: The subsequent synchronised burst of divisions occurs between 20 and 70 μm back from the edge of small wounds and extends beyond 100 μm across the whole field of view for large wounds (Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 3F and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: In the unwounded pupal epithelium, there is a small orientation bias at 45° to the proximal/distal axis.
source: However, surprisingly, we observe a small orientation bias at 45° to this axis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Daughter cells undergo later 'shuffling' movements to rearrange their positions after cytokinesis so that the final daughter cell orientations consistently align along with the P/D axis.
source: Interestingly, our subsequent analysis revealed that daughter cells undergo later 'shuffling' movements to rearrange their positions after cytokinesis so that the final daughter cell orientations (using centres of the cell shapes) consistently align along with the P/D axis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Using U-NetBoundary leads to a much better dice score than using a single focal plane without deep learning.
source: Table 2 shows that using U-NetBoundary leads to a much better dice score and so is more reliable than using a single focal plane without deep learning.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: On average, post-division shuffling shifted final daughter cell orientations by 14.8°.
source: We found that, on average, post-division shuffling shifted final daughter cell orientations by 14.8°.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: The mean orientation relative to the P/D axis had shifted by 8.5° to align with the global tension after post-shuffling.
source: When we measured the post-shuffling orientation relative to the wing's P/D axis, we found that the distribution had shifted to acquire a small bias in the direction of the tension in the tissue (Figure 4B), and the mean orientation relative to the P/D axis had shifted by 8.5° to align with the global tension.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: There is no correlation between division orientation within space and time in unwounded tissue.
source: To examine if this was the case, we measured the correlation between division orientation within space and time, but found no such correlation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Global tension has a small influence on division orientation, but only after shuffling (repositioning) of the daughter cells.

claim: There is no significant shift in the cell orientations post-shuffling following wounding.
